divisionRevenue.title: Revenue by division
divisionRevenue.content:
L'Oréal reports four operating divisions: Luxe (prestige fragrance, makeup and skincare -- YSL, Lancôme, Giorgio Armani), Consumer Products (mass-market -- L'Oréal Paris, Garnier, Maybelline), Dermatological Beauty (pharmacy/physician-recommended -- La Roche-Posay, CeraVe, Vichy), and Professional Products (salon channel -- L'Oréal Professionnel, Redken).

For L'Oréal: Dermatological Beauty has been the fastest-growing division for most of the last decade (CeraVe's mass-channel expansion in the US), while Luxe is the largest and most travel-retail-exposed. The Body Shop (divested 2015) is excluded -- only two years of data exist for it.

What to watch:

  • Dermatological Beauty's share of group revenue over time
  • Luxe growth versus Chinese/travel-retail demand cycles
  • Consumer Products as the slower-growing, highest-volume base

divisionMargin.title: Operating margin by division
divisionMargin.content:
Each division's own operating profit divided by its own revenue, as disclosed in the segment note -- not the group operating margin shown elsewhere on this page.

For L'Oréal: Dermatological Beauty and Luxe typically carry the highest divisional margins; Professional Products (the smallest division, salon-channel) and Consumer Products run thinner. A widening gap between the best- and worst-margin divisions shows where mix shift helps or hurts the group margin.

What to watch:

  • Whether margin gains are mix (faster growth in high-margin divisions) or genuine cost discipline within a division
  • Professional Products' margin trend -- the salon channel was hit hardest by COVID closures

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For L'Oréal S.A.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For L'Oréal S.A.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For L'Oréal S.A.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For L'Oréal S.A.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
